question: According to the Alaska CDL Manual, what fraction of truck driver deaths in crashes result from truck rollovers?
choice_a: More than half
choice_b: About one-quarter
choice_c: Less than ten percent
choice_d: Nearly all
explanation: The manual states, "More than half of truck driver deaths in crashes are the result of truck rollovers."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-1

question: How much more likely are fully loaded rigs to roll over in a crash compared to empty rigs, according to the manual?
choice_a: Twice as likely
choice_b: Ten times as likely
choice_c: Five times as likely
choice_d: They are equally likely
explanation: The manual states, "Fully loaded rigs are ten times more likely to roll over in a crash than empty rigs."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-1

question: Which two things does the manual say will help prevent rollover?
choice_a: Increase tire pressure and use engine braking
choice_b: Reduce trailer length and add extra axles
choice_c: Keep cargo close to the ground and drive slowly around turns
choice_d: Use the trailer hand brake and steer quickly
explanation: The manual says the two things that help prevent rollover are keeping cargo as close to the ground as possible and driving slowly around turns.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-1

question: What does a rearward amplification value of 2.0 mean for a combination vehicle in a quick lane change?
choice_a: The tractor is twice as likely to roll as the trailer
choice_b: The rig can turn 2.0 degrees more sharply than a single vehicle
choice_c: The vehicle needs 2.0 seconds longer to stop
choice_d: The rear trailer is twice as likely to turn over as the tractor
explanation: The manual explains that "rearward amplification of 2.0 in the chart means that the rear trailer is twice as likely to turn over as the tractor."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-1

question: According to the manual, what is the rearward amplification of triples during a quick lane change?
explanation: The manual states, "triples have a rearward amplification of 3.5," meaning you can roll the last trailer of triples 3.5 times as easily as a five-axle tractor.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-1

question: What following distance does the manual recommend when pulling trailers?
choice_a: A fixed 5 seconds regardless of speed or length
choice_b: At least 1 second for each 10 feet of vehicle length, plus another second if going over 40 mph
choice_c: 1 second for each 20 feet of vehicle length only
choice_d: 2 seconds minimum with no adjustment for speed
explanation: The manual advises following "at least 1 second for each 10 feet of your vehicle length, plus another second if going over 40 mph."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-1

question: According to the manual, how do bobtail tractors compare to a fully loaded tractor-semitrailer when stopping?
choice_a: Bobtails stop in about the same distance
choice_b: Bobtails stop more quickly and smoothly
choice_c: Bobtails take longer to stop than a tractor-semitrailer loaded to maximum gross weight
choice_d: Bobtails cannot be tested for stopping ability
explanation: The manual states bobtails "can be very hard to stop smoothly" and that "it takes them longer to stop than a tractor-semitrailer loaded to maximum gross weight."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-1

question: What is the earliest and best way to recognize that a trailer has started to skid, according to the manual?
choice_a: Feeling the steering wheel pull
choice_b: Hearing the tires screech
choice_c: Watching the air pressure gauge drop
choice_d: Seeing it in your mirrors
explanation: The manual states, "The earliest and best way to recognize that the trailer has started to skid is by seeing it in your mirrors."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-2

question: What should you do to stop a trailer skid, and what should you avoid doing?
choice_a: Release the brakes to regain traction, and do not use the trailer hand brake to straighten out the rig
choice_b: Apply the trailer hand brake to straighten the rig
choice_c: Accelerate gently to pull the trailer straight
choice_d: Turn the steering wheel sharply into the skid
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to release the brakes to get traction back, and specifically warns not to use the trailer hand brake to straighten out the rig since the trailer brakes caused the skid in the first place.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-3

question: In a combination vehicle with more than one trailer, which wheels off-track the most, according to the manual?
choice_a: The steer axle wheels
choice_b: The rear wheels of the last trailer
choice_c: The rear wheels of the powered unit (tractor)
choice_d: All wheels off-track equally
explanation: The manual states, "If there is more than one trailer, the rear wheels of the last trailer will off-track the most."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-3

question: When backing a trailer, which way should you turn the steering wheel to make the trailer go where you want?
choice_a: The same direction as you would for a car
choice_b: Only the bottom of the wheel should be turned
choice_c: The opposite direction from backing a car
choice_d: It does not matter which direction
explanation: The manual explains that when backing a trailer, you turn the steering wheel in the opposite direction from what you would use to back a car, straight truck, or bus.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-3

question: What does the manual say the trailer hand valve (trolley valve or Johnson bar) should be used for?
choice_a: Normal driving braking
choice_b: Parking the trailer overnight
choice_c: Emergency steering assistance
choice_d: Only to test the trailer brakes
explanation: The manual states, "The trailer hand valve should be used only to test the trailer brakes. Do not use it in driving because of the danger of making the trailer skid."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-4

question: In what air pressure range will the tractor protection valve close automatically, according to the manual?
choice_a: 20 to 45 psi
choice_b: 5 to 10 psi
choice_c: 50 to 70 psi
choice_d: 80 to 100 psi
explanation: The manual states the tractor protection valve "will close automatically if air pressure is low (in the range of 20 to 45 psi)."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-5

question: On newer vehicles, what does the manual say the trailer air supply control looks like, and how do you use it?
choice_a: A blue round button; push it in to shut off air
choice_b: A red eight-sided knob; push it in to supply air, pull it out to shut off air and apply trailer emergency brakes
choice_c: A green square switch; pull it out to supply air
choice_d: A black lever with no specific shape requirement
explanation: The manual describes the trailer air supply control on newer vehicles as "a red eight-sided knob, which you use to control the tractor protection valve. You push it in to supply the trailer with air, and pull it out to shut the air off and put on the trailer emergency brakes."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-5

question: According to the manual, what colors are used to help avoid connecting the wrong glad hands?
choice_a: Green for service lines and yellow for emergency lines
choice_b: Red for service lines and blue for emergency lines
choice_c: Blue for service lines and red for emergency (supply) lines
choice_d: Black for both lines with no color coding
explanation: The manual states, "Blue is used for the service lines and red for the emergency (supply) lines."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-5

question: How often does the manual say you should drain each trailer air tank?
choice_a: Once a week
choice_b: Once a month
choice_c: Only when the automatic drain fails
choice_d: Every day
explanation: The manual states, "Each tank has a drain valve on it and you should drain each tank every day."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-6

question: According to the manual, which trailers and converter dollies are NOT required to have spring brakes?
choice_a: Those built before 1975
choice_b: Those built after 1998
choice_c: All doubles and triples regardless of age
choice_d: Only trailers used for livestock
explanation: The manual states, "converter dollies and trailers built before 1975 are not required to have spring brakes."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-6

question: As of what date does the manual say all trailers and converter dollies are required to have ABS?
choice_a: January 1, 1995
choice_b: March 1, 1998
choice_c: July 1, 2000
choice_d: January 1, 2005
explanation: The manual states, "All trailers and converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have ABS."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-7

question: What color is the ABS malfunction lamp on trailers, and on which side is it located, according to the manual?
choice_a: Red, on the right side
choice_b: Green, on the front bumper
choice_c: Yellow, on the left side
choice_d: Blue, on the rear only
explanation: The manual states trailers "will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-7

question: According to the manual, does ABS increase or decrease your normal braking capability?
choice_a: It increases normal braking capability
choice_b: It decreases normal braking capability
choice_c: It replaces normal brakes entirely
choice_d: It does not increase or decrease normal braking capability; it only activates when wheels are about to lock up
explanation: The manual states, "ABS is an addition to your normal brakes. It does not decrease or increase your normal braking capability. ABS only activates when wheels are about to lock up."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-7

question: Does ABS necessarily shorten your stopping distance, according to the manual?
choice_a: No, but it helps you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking
choice_b: Yes, it always shortens stopping distance significantly
choice_c: Yes, but only on wet roads
choice_d: No, ABS has no effect on braking at all
explanation: The manual states, "ABS does not necessarily shorten your stopping distance, but it does help you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-7

question: Why does the manual warn against backing the tractor under the trailer at an angle during coupling?
choice_a: It could cause the fifth wheel to overheat
choice_b: It could push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear
choice_c: It could disconnect the electrical cord
choice_d: It could trigger the ABS malfunction lamp
explanation: The manual instructs, "Never back under the trailer at an angle because you might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-8

question: What problem can occur if the trailer is too low when coupling, according to the manual?
choice_a: The kingpin will bend permanently
choice_b: The glad hands will not seal
choice_c: The tractor may strike and damage the trailer nose
choice_d: The landing gear will not raise
explanation: The manual notes that "if the trailer is too low, the tractor may strike and damage the trailer nose; if the trailer is too high, it may not couple correctly."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-8

question: Why does the manual warn against driving with the landing gear only part way up?
choice_a: It voids the tractor protection valve warranty
choice_b: It causes the ABS lamp to malfunction
choice_c: It increases rearward amplification
choice_d: It could catch on railroad tracks or other things
explanation: The manual warns, "Never drive with landing gear only part way up as it may catch on railroad tracks or other things."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-9

question: When inspecting the coupling, where should the fifth wheel's locking jaws be positioned around the kingpin, according to the manual?
choice_a: Around the shank of the kingpin, not the head
choice_b: Around the head of the kingpin
choice_c: Anywhere on the kingpin is acceptable
choice_d: Below the kingpin, not touching it
explanation: The manual's coupling-system inspection checklist specifies checking that the "locking jaws around the shank, not the head of kingpin."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-13
